title: Hierarchical recurrent networks with multiple time scales
matchup: El Hihi and Bengio (1995) vs Schmidhuber (1991, 1992)
question: Does the 1991-93 history-compressor work support Schmidhuber's objection to crediting the 1995 paper with introducing recurrent hierarchies of time scales?

usual_credit.summary: El Hihi and Bengio's 1995 paper studies recurrent layers updating at different fixed rates, using delays and subsampling to address long-term dependencies. Bengio's archived research page describes that paper as introducing a hierarchy of time scales against vanishing gradients, which is the statement Schmidhuber challenges. The paper itself cites his 1992 history-compression work as related, rather than claiming there were no earlier recurrent hierarchies. Chung, Ahn and Bengio's later hierarchical multiscale model also identifies both research lines as early influences while distinguishing fixed update rates from self-organizing time scales.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that his April 1991 sequence-chunker report and its 1992 journal paper already used a hierarchy of recurrent networks to handle long time lags. Each level passes upward only inputs it cannot predict, so slower levels organize their own time scales rather than receiving fixed update rates. He therefore objects to Bengio's later research-page statement that the 1995 paper introduced hierarchies of time scales for this problem. His priority claim concerns the general use of such a hierarchy, while the two papers use different rules for deciding when higher levels update.

response.summary: El Hihi and Bengio's 1995 paper explicitly says Schmidhuber (1992) presented a related hierarchical idea, although it does not cite the 1991 report. A 2001 chapter co-authored by Bengio and Schmidhuber discusses both approaches, and Chung, Ahn and Bengio's later paper calls both early attempts that inspired its model. It distinguishes Schmidhuber's self-organizing hierarchy from fixed layer rates. These acknowledgments limit any claim that the earlier work went wholly uncited, while leaving Bengio's archived use of introduced open to the priority objection. They are source statements, not a direct reply to Schmidhuber's 2020 complaint.

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber's report 'Neural sequence chunkers' (FKI-148-91) is dated April 1991, its abstract says that only the input events not expected by the first recurrent net are transferred to the second, and the paper based on it appeared in Neural Computation 4(2):234-242 in March 1992: https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/FKI-148-91ocr.pdf

El Hihi and Bengio's 'Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Networks for Long-Term Dependencies' was presented at NIPS 1995 and appears on pages 493-499 of Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 8: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1995/hash/c667d53acd899a97a85de0c201ba99be-Abstract.html

The 1995 paper cites Schmidhuber's 1992 paper in its introduction and reference list and does not cite the 1991 report: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1995/file/c667d53acd899a97a85de0c201ba99be-Paper.pdf

In the 1995 paper the time scales are set by the architecture through discrete delays and subsampling, and its experiments train networks with one to six time scales by backpropagation through time on artificial tasks with sequences of up to 100 steps: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1995/file/c667d53acd899a97a85de0c201ba99be-Paper.pdf

The 1991 report frames the problem as long time lags that make backpropagated error signals less significant, says that its systems have no pre-wired decay rate and learn their own time scales, and includes a prediction task with a 20-step time lag: https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/FKI-148-91ocr.pdf

Bengio's research page said that the NIPS 1995 paper introduced the use of a hierarchy of time scales to combat the vanishing gradients issue in captures of 12 April 2020 and 23 December 2022, and Schmidhuber hosts a copy retrieved on 15 May 2020: https://web.archive.org/web/20200412034718/https://yoshuabengio.org/research/ https://web.archive.org/web/20221223013245/https://yoshuabengio.org/research/ https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/ResearchYoshuaBengioMay2020text.html
crux: The dispute is whether a hierarchy of time scales in which a slower recurrent network receives only the inputs that a faster network failed to predict, and in which the time scales organize themselves, counts as the same use of a hierarchy of time scales against long-term dependency problems as El Hihi and Bengio's networks. Their layers update at fixed rates set by delays and subsampling. A narrower question is whether the word 'introduced' on Bengio's research page fits, given that the 1995 paper itself cites the 1992 paper as presenting a related hierarchical idea.
